generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, your practice and work-based learning is usually assessed through a reflective account or log, not through the placement itself. In sport therapy and rehabilitation this matters most: supervisors and tutors, guided by professional standards, look for evidence that you can reflect on your own practice. They want to see what a clinic session revealed about how you work, how it connects to theory and to safe practice, and what you will change. The account is the thing that is marked, not the hours on placement.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport therapy students submit a reflective account of the same rehabilitation placement.

Tom writes a clear, orderly account of what the placement involved: the clinic, the daily routine, the treatments he observed. It reads well and is accurate. But it is a description. It tells the assessor what happened and little about what Tom learned, so there is almost nothing to credit as reflection or insight.

Amara writes less about the routine and more about what it revealed. She describes one session where she misjudged a patient's readiness to progress an exercise, reflects on her part in it, links it to a guideline on load progression she had studied, and sets out what she now does differently. The account shows evidenced insight into her own practice. That is what the criteria reward.

Both students did the same placement and wrote to the same length. Only Amara articulated the learning, which is what is actually assessed.
generatedProse.summary: Practice- and work-based learning in the School of Sport is assessed through reflection because every setting differs: what is marked is the learning you articulate, not the placement itself. A strong reflective account moves beyond description to evidenced insight, honest reflection, a link to theory or professional standards, and a specific change you will make. You can now explain how this learning is assessed, articulate your own learning, and judge an account against what assessors look for. You can turn any sport experience into learning you can show.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's account stronger than Tom's?

items.text: It showed evidenced insight into her own learning, not just a description of events.
It described the placement in more detail.
It was written more clearly and was better organised.
It was longer than Tom's account.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara's account showed evidenced insight into her own learning.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara's account showed beyond a description of events.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's account was stronger because it showed evidenced insight into her learning. Detail, clarity and length were not the difference.
